name: Ivan Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can give me the public answer and the private one too. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We keep 40,000 free-range laying hens in four sheds, for the Brennans, and I start at half six. First job is walking every shed: checking the water lines, the feeders, picking up floor eggs, taking out any dead birds. Then the eggs come down the belts to the packing room, and the grading machine sorts them by size. I keep that machine running, clear jams, stack trays. In the afternoon I let the birds out and check the fences for foxes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the morning walk, when it's quiet and the birds are settling. I don't like the dust, or a jam in the grader when the lorry's due. I'm single and I rent a room from an older lady in the village, Mrs Lund, so my rent's cheap, but I've still only got a few weeks saved. I want a place of my own one day, and a family. Right now that feels a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine. The grading machine's been doing the clever bit for years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the machines we've got already do the job, and AI didn't add much. At work I'd say to Mr Brennan, good, no need to spend money on new gadgets. Online I don't post much, just football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but my problems would still be my problems. Egg prices are set by the big supermarkets, feed costs keep rising, and bird flu can wipe out a shed in a week. A clever computer wasn't going to fix bird flu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep learning the grader and the sheds. I'd use the chat thing sometimes, like when I asked it how to fix a sensor on the water line, and then rang the engineer anyway. I'd ask Mr Brennan if I could do the poultry welfare course, to show I'm serious about the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a normal year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've seen a lot of automation already. How did the grader change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before it, there were four people hand-sorting eggs. Now there's me and the machine. The other three moved on, two to the factory in town, one retired. Nobody starved, and that's why I'm not scared of machines, as long as there's other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make your life better in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit more pay, so I could save for a deposit. I don't want handouts, I just want the work to pay enough for a man to get started. My dad bought his first house at 25. I'm 27 and I rent a room.

S0.say: I'd say the machines we've already got do the job, and AI didn't add much. At work I'd tell the boss there's no need to spend money on new gadgets.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, but the problems stay the same: supermarket egg prices, rising feed costs and bird flu. A clever computer wasn't going to fix bird flu.
S0.do: Keeps learning the grader and the sheds and uses the AI chat tool sometimes before calling the engineer. Asks his employer to send him on a poultry welfare course to show he's serious.
S0.quote: My dad bought his first house at 25. I'm 27 and I rent a room.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan has already lived through automation: the egg grader replaced three hand-sorters, and he saw them find other work. That shapes his calm view of machines, as long as other work exists. His real frustration is that full-time work doesn't pay enough to start a family home, and he's firm that he wants pay, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change. Okay. There are robots for egg farms already, the ones that pick up floor eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines have always changed farming and people adjusted, so we will too. At work I'd tell Mr Brennan to wait and see what the big farms do first. With friends I'd say, learn the new kit and you'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the floor-egg robot takes my morning walk and the dead-bird job. That's half my day. But somebody has to fix the robots and the grader, and I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a farm near us had the shed robot running for a season. Then I'd ask to be trained on it, and I'd try the chat thing more to understand the settings. I'd also start putting £100 a month aside, which means cutting the takeaways and the match tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when there's bird flu two counties away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bird flu two counties away. Tell me about that feeling.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You check the sheds twice as often, you wash your boots ten times, and you still don't sleep properly. It's not here, but it might be. That's what this feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say work hard and learn the machine, the way he did. My mum would say go to services and keep your head. Both good advice, really.

S1.say: Machines have always changed farming and people adjusted, so we will too. I'd tell the boss to wait and see what the big farms do, and tell friends to learn the new kit.
S1.think: The floor-egg robot takes my morning walk and the dead-bird job, which is half my day. But somebody has to fix the robots and the grader, and I'd like to be that person.
S1.do: Waits until a nearby farm has run a shed robot for a season, then asks to be trained on it and uses the AI chat tool more to learn the settings. Saves £100 a month by cutting takeaways and match tickets.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing bird flu is two counties away.
S1.quote: It's not here, but it might be. That's what this feels like.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's steady approach shows clearly: watch a nearby farm for a season, then learn. His comparison to bird flu nearby was vivid and fits his world. His parents' advice mixes hard work and faith, which he values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's too fast for anyone to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this time is different, because before there was always other work and now there isn't. At work I'd say we need to look after each other. I'd want the government to help businesses keep people on, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the egg farm runs itself and I'm out by 2028. The factory in town, where the grader lads went, will be robots too. So where do I go? I don't know, and that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop spending on anything I don't need, and save every penny. I'd ask Mrs Lund if I could do odd jobs for her instead of some of the rent. I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a small shop, about working there. And I'd go to my parents and the community for help before going to the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be losing sleep, like the bird flu was in our sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'help businesses keep people on, not hand out money'. Why that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because work gives a man dignity. Handouts don't. I'd rather Mr Brennan was paid to keep me on, doing something, than me sitting at home with a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans for a home and family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On hold. You can't ask a girl to marry you when you don't have a job and the world's upside down. I'd wait.

S2.say: This time is different, because before there was always other work and now there isn't. I'd want the government to help businesses keep people on, not just hand out money.
S2.think: The egg farm runs itself and I'm out by 2028. The factory where the grader lads went will be robots too, so I don't know where I'd go, and that's frightening.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending and offers his landlady odd jobs in place of some rent. Asks his uncle about work in his small shop and turns to his parents and community before the government.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, as if bird flu were in his own sheds.
S2.quote: This time is different, because before there was always other work and now there isn't.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan's calm view of automation rested on there always being other work, and the two-year picture removes that. He wants policy that keeps people in jobs rather than cash payments, tied to his belief that work gives dignity. His plans to marry would go on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, so let's make one, not panic. At work I'd say let's learn the new machines as they come. With friends I'd say, get a trade that's useful while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get maybe three years of being the one who keeps the robots going. Then the robots fix themselves and it's the same problem. But three years of good wages could get me a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the welfare course and ask for training on any robot Mr Brennan buys. I'd save hard, £150 a month if I can, maybe more if I take on weekend shifts. By year three I'd look at an electrical apprenticeship, because my cousin did one and he's never short of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship rather than a college course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you learn from a man who does it, and you get paid while you learn. That's how my dad learnt his trade. A college course is someone talking at you and a debt at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still put off marriage in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. Five years is long enough to get started. If I met the right person, I'd want to get married and have a home before it all hits.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make a plan, so let's make one, not panic. I'd say at work that we should learn the new machines as they come, and tell friends to get a useful trade.
S3.think: I'd get maybe three years of keeping the robots going before they fix themselves. But three years of good wages could get me a deposit.
S3.do: Takes the welfare course and robot training in year one and saves £150 a month, more with weekend shifts. By year three looks at an electrical apprenticeship like his cousin's.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to see a way through.
S3.quote: A college course is someone talking at you and a debt at the end.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Ivan returns to his steady plan: learn the machines, save hard, then an apprenticeship. He prefers learning on the job from someone experienced over college, which fits his values. More time also brings back his hopes of marriage and a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. My dad's age when I was ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to adapt properly, the way farmers always have. At work I'd tell the younger ones to get a trade. With friends I'd say don't wait for the government, sort yourself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels okay. I'd get married, have a home, maybe kids. But I'd be thinking about what they'll do when they grow up, if robots do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years I'd stay on the egg farm and save, and learn the robots as they come in. Around year three I'd start an electrical apprenticeship, and finish by year six or seven. I'd want a house by 35 and a few months' savings, so whatever happens in 2036, my family's okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a good season with no disease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't wait for the government. Is there anything you'd want from them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paying for apprenticeships, maybe. And keeping taxes low so people can save. Beyond that, I think families and towns should look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you leave it too late in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Ten years is long enough to get comfortable. But I'd have my dad on the phone asking about it every Sunday, so I don't think he'd let me forget.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to adapt properly, the way farmers always have. I'd tell the younger ones to get a trade and tell friends not to wait for the government.
S4.think: Ten years feels okay: I'd marry, have a home and maybe kids. But I'd wonder what they'll do when they grow up if robots do everything.
S4.do: Stays on the egg farm, saves and learns the robots for the first few years, then completes an electrical apprenticeship by year six or seven. Aims for a house by 35 and a few months' savings before 2036.
S4.feel: Calm, like a good season with no disease.
S4.quote: I'd have my dad on the phone asking about it every Sunday, so I don't think he'd let me forget.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Ivan plan in the order he values: steady work, a trade, then marriage and a home. He wants government help limited to funding apprenticeships and low taxes. He admits he might get comfortable and wait too long, and counts on his father to keep him moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Before, when the grader came, the lads found other work. In two years there wouldn't be any other work to find. What would help is the government paying businesses to keep people on and paying for real apprenticeships, so people have dignity and something to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. When everything's changing, people need something steady. For me it's my family and going to services. I think that matters more than people say.

headlineQuote: This time is different, because before there was always other work and now there isn't.
portrait: Ivan Haddad is a 27-year-old junior worker on a 40,000-hen egg farm, walking the sheds each morning and keeping the grading machine running. He's single, rents a room from an older woman in the village and wants a home and family of his own. He has already seen automation: the grader replaced three hand-sorters, and they found other work, which kept him calm about machines. In AGI by 2028 that comfort breaks, because there would be no other work to find. With more time he follows a steady path of robot training, saving and an electrical apprenticeship, and he values work and family over handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because unlike past automation there would be no other work to move into.
whatWouldHelp: Government help for businesses to keep people on, and funding for real apprenticeships, so people keep their dignity.
